Over the past week, calls for mass surveillance and censorship have reached a
fever pitch.

On Wednesday, Australia's[ highly controversial social media
ban](https://www.nbcnews.com/world/asia/australia-launches-youth-social-media-
ban-rcna246730), which blocked
[millions](https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2025/dec/09/australia-
under-16-social-media-ban-begins-apps-listed) of users from large swaths of
the internet, went into effect. So far, it has had devastating consequences.

[Subscribe now](https://zeteo.com/subscribe)

Countless adults who are unable or unwilling to link their government ID to
their online activity or comply with age verification requirements another way
can't access major social platforms; calls to a youth suicide prevention help
line [reportedly up](https://x.com/DrDemography/status/1998601576483795164) as
teens were cut off from their online support networks and communities; kids
[began downloading](https://x.com/cameronwilson/status/1998462449628979341)
unregulated and potentially more dangerous apps en masse; and it was revealed
that a [primary advocacy
group](https://www.crikey.com.au/2025/12/11/36-months-leaked-document-teen-
social-media-ban/) behind the ban's passage was developing an AI tool to track
students and was funded and co-staffed by a firm that was [simultaneously
making gambling ads](https://www.crikey.com.au/2025/12/12/pro-teen-social-
media-ban-group-funded-firm-making-gambling-ads/).

Despite the chaos and abject harm the law in Australia has wrought, US
lawmakers are eagerly seeking to replicate it.
